newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Companies rally to global pact on Internet names.
newsitem.headline: Companies rally to global pact on Internet names.

text.p: A bloc of global and national companies and cyberspace bodies, brushing aside reservations from the United States and the European Union, on Thursday set up a new structure for registering addresses on the Internet.

A total of 56 entities, with 23 pledging they would follow, signed an accord creating the new system which its designers say will establish self-governance for the Internet and bring competition to the lucrative "domain name" business.

The accord, a memorandum of understanding, is aimed at ending confusion over allocation of "top-level domain" names or TLDs, counterparts of telephone numbers on the rapidly expanding Internet which is now used by an estimated 50 million people.

It will end a monopoly currently held by the U.S.-based Network Solutions Inc (NSI) on so-called "generic" TLDs -- .com, .org and .net -- by creating seven more like .store for shops, .arts for culture and .nom for individual web sites.
Geographic addresses, like .fr for France and .ch for Switzerland, are assigned by national registrars.

The signing came at the end of a three-day conference, described by Internet Society President Don Heath as "a raving success", under the umbrella of two Geneva-based United Nations agencies closely involved in new technology, ITU and WIPO.

ITU, the International Telecommunications Union, and WIPO, the World Intellectual Property Organisation -- will act respectively as the depositor for the accord and administrator of its dispute settlement mechanism.

U.S. officials have made clear they believe the project, drafted by an International Ad Hoc Committee (IAHC) from the Internet community, the ITU and WIPO, needed more preparation and consultation before implementation.
Similar views were expressed at the conference by an EU representative.

But Heath, an Internet pioneer, told a news conference that governmental bodies were bound to take a cautious approach. "I fully believe we will eventually have the endorsement of the U.S. administration," he said.

MCI Communications Inc, one of the major companies backing the new system and a key Internet service provider, said the plan would ensure that Internet self-governance kept pace with its rapid commercial and technological advancement.

Other business signatories include the U.S. Digital Corp, and national telecommunications companies ranging from Sweden and Italy to Albania. The French state-owned France Telecom has said it will join in shortly.

Heath said several entities who came to the conference either sceptical or opposed to the project were won round when they learned it was an evolving system which they could help to shape and improve in the coming years.
"We didn't lose anybody, and in fact we gained some. So the momentum is there," he said.

The accord will initially set up a network of 28 new registrars over the coming months for addresses under the new TLDs, equally distributed around the seven regions of the world, to be selected by a lottery system.

Internet users wanting to open a new site will be able to apply to any of these, ensuring prices remain competitive in a business that has brought hefty revenues to NSI which charges $100 for each registration.

NSI has insisted the three core TLDs will remain its property when an authorisation from the U.S. National Science Federation to administer them runs out next March and has expressed strong opposition to the new system.

This has opened the prospect for possible legal conflict, but Heath said he and his colleagues were not looking for a clash. "We would like NSI to come in with us and take a leadership role in developing the new system," he said.
